claims.text: Enhanced surface segregation of low-melting-point elements lowers the activation barrier for premelting and overall melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface segregation produces a depressed melting onset relative to nanoparticles with homogeneous surfaces.
The initial near-equiatomic nanoparticles possess inherent atomic-scale heterogeneity.
Pre-annealing or chemical treatment can be used to promote or inhibit surface segregation while retaining an equiatomic bulk composition.
Ni is presented as a low-melting component suitable for surface enrichment.
Premelting is expected to begin at approximately 300–400°C.
Complete melting is expected at approximately 800–1000°C.
The degree of surface segregation and associated local chemical ordering constitute the structural mediator governing melting behavior.
Changes in surface composition significantly alter local surface energy and cohesion.
Induced surface segregation creates surface regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Reduced surface cohesive energy decreases the local melting point.
A lower local melting point causes earlier surface atomic mobility and premelting.
Earlier surface premelting shifts overall melting to lower temperatures than in otherwise identical nanoparticles with homogeneous surfaces.
Segregation-enhancing treatments will lower both the premelting onset temperature and the complete melting temperature relative to untreated homogeneous nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold for nanoparticles of similar size and bulk composition under controlled, oxidation-free conditions from about 300°C through complete melting at about 800–1000°C.
Surface composition profiles can be characterized using XPS or atom probe tomography.
Failure of successfully segregation-enhanced nanoparticles to show statistically significant reductions in both premelting onset and melting temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of the treatment to produce the intended surface-composition change would itself falsify the hypothesis.
